JB 3018

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-12-269990-036

DATE:

August 9, 2005

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

ROGER E. BAKER,
J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

R. K.

Plaintiff

v.

D. D.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The Court has heard a Petition for Divorce,
together with demands by both Plaintiff and Defendant for a variety of
accessory measures.

[
2
]

The Parties were married in Montreal on May 29,
1994, in the City of Montreal.  R. K. the Plaintiff, is now forty five (45)
years of age. She has changed the direction of her proceedings several times,
particularly as they affect the custody of the couple’s two young children,
which she does not seek as sole custodial parent as was the case originally, but
rather asks the Court to now order joint custody  on an alternating weekly
basis.

[
3
]

The original issues between the Parties at the
outset of the proceedings were not unique to cases of this nature: custody,
access rights, the financial consequences of the couple’s life together, and
the subsequent separation.

[
4
]

This was dramatically altered as a consequence
of the raising of the allegation by R. K. approximately nine months after she
initiated these proceedings that her husband D. D. had sexually abused their
son A., and also that he had inappropriately slept naked in bed with his eight
year old daughter S.. He categorically denied these allegations. Thus began the
all out war which ended in a bitterly contested trial.

THE PARTIES

[
5
]

R. K.

Prior to meeting her husband, Mme
K. worked in her parents clothing store in Montreal where she learned styling,
sales, and generally the business of  women’s clothing, in its many  aspects.
The marriage to Mr. D. was her first, at age thirty five. Through the years of
their marriage, she worked for her husband’s company and became an accomplished
sales person, travelling widely while bringing up two small children. These
business travels were both alone or with her husband.

[
6
]

D. D.

Mr. D., now forty four (44) studied economics for
two years at the University of Western Ontario. He left at age 19 to begin work
in the field of textiles which, over time would develop into a very successful
business career. Through the years he has had business partners in Canada, New
York, and Italy. As a result of the allegations of sexual abuse made by Mme K.
against him, which have proven to be entirely without foundation, he has
altered his position as to what he believes to be in the best interests of the
children, and now seeks sole custody.

THE CHILDREN

[
7
]

A. D.

A. D. is now seven years of age. It is
uncontestable that he has had, and continues to have, a troubled childhood. He
has also had considerable difficulties in school, beginning with kindergarten,
and in fact has been asked to leave more than one educational facility for
behavioral problems.  A. continues to require special attention at school and
will continue to do so in the future at home as well.

[
8
]

S. D.

She is now almost nine years of age, and by all
accounts is a normal child, with no special problems.

THE LIFESTYLE OF THE D. FAMILY AT THE TIME OF THE SEPARATION

[
9
]

By
the time of the separation in 2003, this family enjoyed a lifestyle that can be
described as one of luxury. They own a large home in one of Montreal’s most
prestigious neighborhoods, and own as well a country retreat which has been
described as very well furnished at considerable cost. Indeed, the
uncontradicted evidence is to the effect that the cost of the art and furniture
in both homes amounts to several hundred thousand dollars. This family wanted
for very little of the material aspects of living.

TESTIMONY

[
10
]

R. K. (Mme K.) testified at length on the
subject of her children, whose joint custody she seeks, contrary to her earlier
position when she sought sole custody.

[
11
]

She spoke only briefly however of S., now nine
years of age, as a child who is happy and who is successful at school, with
whom she has an excellent relationship. They do many things together, and
according to her mother, S. is “great.”

[
12
]

Describing her son A., age six, as a loving boy,
Mme K., then went on to say that he is “ mad at the world for something” and
tends to bite and scream. These symptoms existed prior to the separation of the
parents; in fact, it began in his pre-school days. His behaviour was so
disruptive that that the parties were asked to take him out of the School A, a
pre-school for very young children.

[
13
]

A. was brought to a Dr. Lalinec who met with him
for approximately ten visits in an attempt to deal with his behaviour. After a
year or so, A. was returned to the School A, but at the age of four and one
half (4 ½) he was asked to leave again.

[
14
]

Mme K. spoke of then bringing A. to School B in Town
A where he stayed for approximately one year, from September 2003; he was not
bluntly asked to leave, but the parents were requested to seek help for their
son.

[
15
]

At that time the parents were already in the
early stages of this present case, and both counsel had recommended Linda
Greenberg the psychologist as a joint expert in the divorce. Greenberg
suggested that A. be sent to the Jewish General Hospital which had facilities
for helping young children with problems similar to those manifested by A.

[
16
]

Greenberg filed an expert’s report (D-52 A) (the
1
st
Greenberg Report) on January 29, 2004, which report was
addressed to the legal counsel of both parents as it was jointly commissioned;
it recommended joint or shared custody between the parents.

[
17
]

After an adversarial hearing, Mme Justice Helene
Lebel, at the request of Mr. D., granted shared custody in a judgment of
February 13, 2004. While this was done on an interim basis, after several
changes in proceedings, strategy and tactics by both parents, this interim
solution has, by consent, endured up to the final hearing.

[
18
]

Mme K. addressed the subject of the allegations
of inappropriate sexual activity by her husband with both their children.

[
19
]

She said that subsequent to the judgment of
Lebel j., S. started sleeping in her father’s bed when he was exercising his
part of the shared custody. Mme K. stated that Mr D. slept naked, and as a
consequence she had her legal counsel address a letter to Mr. D.’s counsel on
March 11, 2004 suggesting the impropriety of this kind of activity.

[
20
]

When questioned by the Court, Mme K. admitted
that her husband always slept naked, and furthermore S. herself slept in the
same bed with her parents from time to time and did so without any clothing. It
would appear the mother never complained prior to the letter referred to above.

[
21
]

In a somewhat surprising statement, Mme K.
admitted that there was nothing inappropriate or wrong with S., then seven
years of age, sleeping naked with her father.

[
22
]

She seemed not to manifest any understanding
that this allegation, coming as it did through her lawyer, might poison the
atmosphere between parents, quite apart from the fact that the story was not
new, and was in fact baseless.

[
23
]

Mme K. then addressed the issue which has become
a critically important element in the custody struggle between these parties.

[
24
]

She testified that she was putting A. to bed in
the Spring of 2004 when he disclosed certain shocking facts which, after she
related them to her legal counsel and on his advice, taped a subsequent
conversation with him. What follows is a certified transcription of that taped
conversation:

I certify that this transcription of a conversation
between Madame R. K. and her son A. was made faithfully and accurately from an
audio tape in our possession supplied by Me Claude Lamarre.

Transcribed by:

(S) Gintautas Kaminskas

Montréal, May 4, 2004

[
25
]

Counsel to Mr. D. affirmed that the above
transcript is faithful to the tape recording. The tape recording of the
conversation was played for the Court.

[
26
]

A reading of the above indicates that Mme K.,
with the form of her questions as well as her insistence, intended to lead this
six year old child to the answers she required. She succeeded. There is no
spontaneity in his answers; furthermore she repeatedly refers the child to a
previous conversation and virtually forces him to repeat a conversation to
which the listener to the tape is not privy.

[
27
]

Mme K. appears to have had an aversion to
calling in the medical profession when the condition of her son appeared to warrant
it. She stated that in the period of the trial, A. was “starting to dig in his
bum.” She went on to say that “it’s all over the place.”

[
28
]

Surprisingly, Mme K. stated that she spoke to no
doctors about this, notwithstanding that it had been going on for approximately
one and one half months.

[
29
]

She was asked why she accepted the opinion of
two experts, Drs. David and Van Gijseghem, who concluded that her husband did
not engage in the practice as described in the above transcript. Her response
was that they are professionals, and accordingly she accepts their findings.
Apparently it hadn’t occurred to her to consult any professional other than a
lawyer when this shocking revelation was made by her son. Mme K. then revealed
her true nature in saying: I accepted their findings “ so if my son ever comes
back to me, I can say—I did what I had to do.”

[
30
]

Mme K. neglected to take appropriate measures
when first confronted with these allegations by A., if indeed he actually
raised the issue as his mother has testified, nor was she taking measures
during the period of the trial when A. was manifesting behaviour indicating
some disorder that might well have been referred to a member of the medical
profession.

[
31
]

This testimony by Mme K., as well as her
behaviour prior to trial on the subject of the sexual abuse by her husband
against his own children lacked credibility, and had the indicia of a
deliberate attempt to blacken his reputation to further some venial but
obviously unstated purpose, on which the Court cannot speculate.

[
32
]

The cross examination of Mme K. revealed an
inconsistency in her concern for her son A.: as noted above, she first called
her lawyer when A. would have made the allegations, and upon advice of counsel
she taped a conversation with him as described above. She testified “I did not
call the kid’s pediatrician,” and immediately and without prompting stated that
she did return the children to their father the following  weekend when his
turn came.

[
33
]

Either Mme K. believed A. or she did not. It
cannot be ignored that we are considering the actions of the mother of a six
year old boy, who had, at that point , a history of quite troubled behaviour.

[
34
]

Yet when the allegation was made, she took
absolutely no protective steps to assure that A. would be safe; however she
would only have to do this in the event she thought the allegation either be
true, or that something was untowards between her husband and son.

[
35
]

She did nonetheless without apparent fear return
her son A. to his father that weekend when it was his turn. Either D. D. was
thought by Mme K. to be a pervert or he was not. It is inconceivable that any
intelligent and loving mother would, without some immediate attempt to avoid placing
her child in harms way, simply return him to the source of potentially serious
and harmful contact with his father, given the gravity of the allegations.

[
36
]

That she did so leads the Court to conclude on
this subject either that she didn’t believe the story if indeed it originated
with A. in the first instance, or that it was a fiction which Mme K. used
repeatedly and deliberately in proceedings, affidavits, and amended proceedings
in an effort to blacken the name of and gain advantage over D. D., her husband.
Mme K.’s testimony and her activities prior to trial as noted above are entirely
lacking in credibility.

TESTIMONY OF D. D. ON THE CHILDREN

[
37
]

In describing the birth of his daughter S., Mr. D.
said he had been very excited by the birth; “that’s why I got married - to have
a family.” This differs dramatically from the version given by Mme K. who
testified that her husband was not at all pleased by the birth of his first
child.

[
38
]

He spoke of S. as an affectionate, outgoing,
smiling little girl, who is quite

sensitive, with a good heart and willing to share with others.

[
39
]

The issue of allegations by Mme K. that the
father of the two children was engaging in inappropriate sexual activity with
both his son and daughter in different circumstances has raised issues that did
not exist at the outset of the present litigation. Allegations of this nature
are not to be dismissed lightly by a court, even when after close examination
by experts find the allegations to be unfounded, but particularly important is
the examination of the manner in which the accusing parent made the
allegations, the possible motives for making them, and most importantly, the
impact of the allegations in the determination of where the best interests of
the children lie, for it is only this latter consideration that must determine
the issue of custody.

[
40
]

The evidence discloses a fractious relationship
between these parents, so much so that virtually all normal communication is
non existant. As noted above, the mother is now asking for joint custody, while
the father, since the allegations of abuse were raised, has changed his position
and seeks sole custody.

[
41
]

D. D., while under oath, testified that the
allegations against him on the matter of sexual impropriety against both his
children, were completely and utterly false. The giving of this evidence
appeared to the Court to be sincere, and was credible.

[
42
]

The Court heard the testimony of two experts on
the subject of custody and visiting or access rights, and as well has had the
benefit of their respective reports on both subjects.

THE EXPERTS REPORTS

[
43
]

Linda L. Greenberg, clinical psychologist—Report
[1]
March 29, 2005
(hereinafter referred to as the Greenberg Report).

[
44
]

Although originally Linda Greenberg filed a
report which was jointly mandated by both parents and recommended joint
custody, Mme K., subsequent to the allegations of sexual abuse withdrew this
mandate from Greenberg who, at the request of Mr. D., filed the final Report
now under discussion as the Greenberg Report.

[
45
]

Greenberg refers to the earliest considerations
of the validity of the allegations of sexual abuse in the following terms:

“Mr. D., for his part, denied the
allegations and contested Ms. K.’s request to modify the joint custody
arrangement and to have his access rights limited or suspended. Moreover,
subsequent to Ms. K. withdrawing the mandate of the undersigned to evaluate the
said allegations and to complete an updated assessment, Mr. D. mandated
psychologist, Monsieur Raymond David, in May 2004 to evaluate the minor
children with respect to the said allegations and to give his expert opinion on
the possible consequences or sequellae of false allegations on the development
of the children.

Both children were interviewed and
assessed with respect to the said allegations, first on May 28, 2004 by
Monsieur David and, subsequently, on June 9, 2004, jointly with Monsieur David
and Dr. Van Gijseghem. Monsieur David also interviewed Mr. D. on two occasions
(June 3 and June 8, 2004) and evaluated him psychometrically. With regard to
Ms. K., Monsieur David stated in his report:

“
Rencontre avec madame R... K... non faite puisque
madame a décliné notre invitation lors d’une conversation téléphonique le 8
juillet 2004.
”

In his report dated July 22, 2004,
Monsieur David, in collaboration with Dr. Van Gijseghem, concluded that, based
on the assessment of the two minor children:

“
… aucun des éléments reliés aux critères de
crédibilité concernant le dévoilement fait par un enfant n’était présent, ni
par la suite, lors des entrevues avec A..., ni lors des entrevues avec S...;
”

and

“
Bien qu’il soit impossible avec une totale certitude
d’éliminer la possibilité d’un abus sexuel, nous pouvons confirmer qu’aucun
indice ne fut relevé lors de ces rencontres
;”

Monsieur David also stated the
following conclusion in his report:

“
Lors de ces rencontres, autant individuelle qu’en
présence de monsieur Van Gijseghem, aucun indice lié à quelque inconduite
sexuelle entre le père et les enfants ne s’est manifesté.
”

With regard to his assessment of
Mr. D., Monsieur David concluded the following:

“il nous semble evident que la relation qui
existe entre monsieur D... D... et ses deux enfants est d’excellente qualit
é;
”

and

“
nous ne croyons pas que le père ait pu avoir une
inconduite sexuelle avec ses deux enfants.
”

On the other hand, with regard to
Ms. K., Monsieur David expressed the following opinion in his report:

“
… lors d’une conversation téléphonique, nous avons
invité madame R... K... à se rendre à nos bureaux pour deux motifs :

1)

pour lui faire
part des informations liées aux rencontres que nous avons eues avec les deux
enfants;

2)

pour que la mère
puisse nous communiquer si elle se sentait confortable et en sécurité dans le
cadre des accès entre les enfants et leur père.

Madame K... a décliné notre invitation, ce qui,
avouons-le, nous laisse un peu perplexe.
”

With regard to the issues of
custody and access rights, Monsieur David stated in his report that, given the
fact that Ms. K. declined his request to meet with her,

“
Dans ces
circonstances, nous ne sommes donc pas en mesure de formuler une recommandation
complète concernant l’organisation ou la réorganisation de la garde et des
accès reliés aux enfants compte tenu du fait que nous n’avons pas eu
l’opportunité de rencontrer la mère.
”

Based on his assessment, however,
he did state the following:

“
… si les allégations d’abus sexuels faisaient partie
d’une campagne d’aliénation parentale orchestrée par la mère, contre le père,
nous sommes en mesure d’évoquer qu’une telle stratégie pourrait être
extrêmement dommageable pour :

➢

la relation des enfants avec leur père et à
cet effet, la littérature scientifique concernant la traumatisme relié à de
fausse allégations d’abus sexuel affirme que «
people who have been
falsely accused of abuse often experience the same type of symptoms as those
who have actually been abused, like trauma, betrayal, powerlessness and
stigmatization
».

➢

le développement psychologique des deux
enfants à moyen et long terme.”

Based on his assessment, he also
opined that:

“
Compte tenu de ce qui nous est rapporté par le père et
si effectivement le dévoilement d’attouchements sexuels a été fait par la mère
parce qu’elle n’aurait pas été d’accord avec les recommandations de l’expert
Greenberg, il faudrait revoir l’organisation de la garde.
”

Based on the court testimony, Ms. K.
remains firm in her allegations that A. disclosed information to her about his
father in a spontaneous and unsolicited manner. She accepts the conclusions of
the experts with respect to the allegations of inappropriate conduct by the
father and, regarding the issue of custody, she is requesting a continuation of
the status quo, believing joint custody on an alternating weekly schedule to be
in the best interests of the children.

In contrast, on the grounds that he
believes that Ms. K. fabricated false allegations of sexual abuse against him,
motivated, in his opinion, by her goal to have sole custody and to limit his
contact and relationship with the children and, furthermore, on the grounds
that she involved the two children directly in her attempt to discredit him and
alienate him from the children, Mr. D. is requesting sole custody, believing it
to be in the best interests of the children.”
[2]

[
46
]

Greenberg thus relied to some extent on the analysis of two experts Drs.
David and Van Gijseghem who examined the children and found the allegations as
reported by Mme K. to be extremely unlikely and thus unfounded. Their
examinations were conducted approximately eight months prior to the second
mandate of Greenberg and therefore  much more contemporaneous to the “events.”

[
47
]

The importance of the work of the two experts David and Van Gijseghem is
that relatively close in time to the alleged events they were satisfied that no
sexual abuse was committed by Mr. D.

[
48
]

The result of the allegations, however false, has created considerable
difficulties in the relationship of the parents. Greenberg notes:

“One of the issues which has
created a great deal of stress and animosity in the family since the completion
of the initial assessment has been the allegations made by Ms. K. that Mr. D.
had behaved inappropriately sexually with both S. and A.. These allegations
were revealed first informally by Ms. K., through her attorney in early April
2004 and, more formally, subsequently in her Déclaration Solennelle of May 19,
2004. Among other allegations of inappropriate behaviour, Ms. K. alleged that S.
was sleeping naked in her father's bed and that A. had allegedly disclosed to
her in March 2004 that his father had put his finger in A.’s anus. The
allegations, which have clearly stirred up a great deal of tension, conflict
and distrust between the parties, were vigorously denied and formally contested
by Mr. D., who alleged that the allegations were fabrications, raised for the
purpose of discrediting him and for causing prejudice to the loving and
respectful relationship between him and the children.

At the present time, based on an
assessment conducted by psychologist, Monsieur Raymond David, in collaboration

and that the Defendant be ordered to transfer to the Plaintif 50% of the shares
of Company A;

Even though the
Plaintiff has requested that her rights be recognized and that 50% of the
shares in Company A presently registered in the name of Defendant, be
transfered to her, this request has been refused;

The Plaintiff
invokes in her favor the articles 229, 239, 240, 241 and following of the
Loi
canadienne sur les sociétés par actions
and this in order to raise the
argument that she was treated unfairly by the Defendant, the sole registered
Shareholder and Director of Company A, and to have declared that she was
treated with abuse of rights without fair play in an abusive, injust,
oppressive, irregular and illegal manner by D. D. and the said Company, the
whole without regard to the reasonable expectations of the Plaintiff;”
[13]

[
71
]

These claims by Plaintiff invoke rights of
partnership between the parties as well as abuse and oppression under the
Canadian Business Corporations Act by the Defendant , and seeks, as seen above,
a judgment ordering a distribution in her favour of 50 % of all
assets(including shares) registered in the name of D. D. which are not part of
the family patrimony.

[
72
]

The evidence before the Court on this claim is
utterly non existent, and to the extent that Mme K. attempted to justify the
claim while under oath, she so lacked  credibility that it can only be observed
that the claim itself is specious and without merit. Mme K. repeatedly suffered
from lapses of memory, was unsure of what it was she did and when while working
as a sales person in the company of her husband, and failed to demonstrate how
her work justifies the claim.

[
73
]

There is no credible evidence before the Court
that the Defendant D. D. ever agreed to any part of division of his personal
assets with his wife.

[
74
]

What is however apparent to the Court is that
Mme R. K. has in the past and continued to do so until she testified indulged
in wishful thinking on the subject of her pretended rights in the assets of
others.

[
75
]

She testified that prior to marriage she worked
in stores owned by her family, and that while she was not an owner on paper,
“mentally I was an owner.” That testimony is indicative of the manner in which
Mme K. calculates her rights. Wishful thinking is not evidence, and moreover,
her mother Si. K. testified but was silent on the issue of her daughter’s
contributions to or rights in the family business.

[
76
]

Thus the claim raised by Plaintiff for a
division of D. D.’s assets is entirely without merit for want of any credible
evidence.

COMPENSATORY ALLOWANCE:

[
77
]

While there is no direct claim in her
proceedings for a compensatory allowance, it has however been raised as a
subsidiary claim in Plaintiff’s Notes and Authorities:

«
Subsidiairement
,
si le tribunal en venait à la conclusion qu’aucune société tacite n’a existé
entre les parties, K. est en droit de demander une prestation compensatoire en
"compensation" de l’enrichissement de D. auquel elle a participé
directement. »
[14]

[
78
]

The criteria under the
law of this province
[15]
for
compensatory allowance are the following:

427.
The court, in declaring separation
from bed and board, divorce or nullity of marriage, may order either spouse to
pay to the other, as compensation for the latter's contribution, in property or
services, to the enrichment of the patrimony of the former, an allowance
payable in cash or by instalments, taking into account, in particular, the
advantages of the matrimonial regime and of the marriage contract.  […]

[…]

428.
The cooperating spouse may adduce
any evidence to prove his or her contribution to the enrichment of the
patrimony of the other spouse.

[
79
]

In a claim for compensatory allowance, as in all claims asserted in
legal proceedings, there is a burdon of proof which must be discharged by the
party asserting the claim. The evidence in this record is clear that Plaintiff
was well paid for the work while with Defendant’s company Company B, and her
earnings contributed to the family patrimony in which she will now share
equally with Defendant, who as a result of his greater earnings, made a much
more significant contribution to this family patrimony.

[
80
]

There is a complete absence of credible evidence that there was an
unjust enrichment by Defendant to the detriment of Plaintiff.

[
81
]

This subsidiary claim for a compensatory allowance must be considered in
the context that Plaintiff has first claimed an ownership position in virtually
all the Defendant’s assets, and it is only in the event of the inability to
succeed with that claim, does she raise the issue of unjust enrichment or
compensation for work that has gone unrewarded for her contribution to her
husband’s fortune.

[
82
]

Plaintiff’s earnings over the years of her nine year marriage have made
an important contribution to the family patrimony; this contribution will be
rewarded by her share in that patrimony, which in accordance with law will be
divided equally between the spouses irrespective of the weight of their
contributions. The evidence is clear in that the Defendant contributed
disproportionally to this patrimony. It is also clear that the Plaintiff was a
sales person working for her husband’s company, and no evidence exists in the
record that it was as a result of her uncompensated work that Company B and
Defendant’s other assets grew as a consequence of her efforts.

[
83
]

For the work she performed, she was well paid, and in part as a result
of this work she will participate in an important sum from the family
patrimony.

LUMP SUM/SPOUSAL SUPPORT CLAIM:

[
84
]

In addition to the above, Plaintiff asserts an additional claim for a
lump sum in the amount of $500,000.00.

[
85
]

It is settled law that a lump sum is awarded on the basis of it being a
form of alimentary allowance, which raises the issue of the needs of the
beneficiary.

[
86
]

Upon the separation in June 2003, Mme K. ceased working for Company B
and shortly thereafter initiated legal proceedings for unjustified dismissal.
Subsequent to the hearing before the undersigned, the parties executed a
Transaction on May 2, 2005 by the terms of which Mme K. was to receive as
compensation the sum of $70,000.00 plus the amount of $10,000.00  for legal
fees.

[
87
]

Mme K. has testified that she worked for her parents prior to this
marriage, and that during the marriage she continued to work with but two brief
absences. She has not sought work since the separation. There would appear to
be no reasonable justification for this lack of effort. By her own testimony,
in the context of her abilty, Mme K. should have been able to re-integrate
herself into the workforce by now. There is no apparent medical reason for her
not to be working.

[
88
]

The purpose of alimentary support for a spouse is to allow for an
orderly re-integration into the work force and to enable the beneficiary to
become self-sufficient.

[
89
]

It should be apparent that upon sale of the family residences and the
distribution of the rest of the family patrimony, in addition to the settlement
from the transaction referred to above, Mme K., with no important financial
responsibility for the children, should be able to live a life without
financial stress.

[
90
]

However, this does not mean that her husband should be entirely
exonerated and freed from aiding in her rehabilitation for a certain period of
time, which under the circumstances should cover a period of two years in an
amount of $4000.00 monthly. Accordingly, the Court will grant to Mme K. the sum
of $100,000.00 as a lump sum payment in lieu of regular payments by Mr. D.
Given the considerable inability of the parties to communicate at any level, it
seems a clean break on matters financial might alleviate at least some of the
difficulties between them. Over time, they will have to try to communicate
better about the welfare of their children.

PROVISION FOR COSTS:

[
91
]

The precise amount of Plaintiff’s legal fees is difficult to ascertain.
Initially at the close of the hearing the Court was advised by Plaintiff’s
counsel that the grand total of all her legal fees amount to approximately
$135,000.00, but that as counsel was prepared to waive part of his fees, the
actual amount being claimed is $112,000.00.

[
92
]

This litigation was turned into an acrimonious and indeed vicious battle
for no good and valid reason. The manner in which Mme K. dealt with the issue
of her husband’s alleged sexual abuse of his son A. and his inappropriate
sleeping arrangements with S. generated unnecessary proceedings which begat
further proceedings by the other side, and so on. Some of these proceedings by
Plaintiff were costly, time consuming, utterly without merit, and it would
seem, as a result of a disastrous divorce strategy calculated to inflame
passions, and entirely without regard to the effect it might have on the
children, short or long term.

[
93
]

The financial aspect of Plaintiff’s proceedings as amended  was
calculated to escalate the war without any credible evidence to justify the
asserted claims, and as a consequence  both parties hereto were required to
expend enormous sums of money to deal with accusations and a claim which was
entirely unjustified.

[
94
]

The responsibility for the enormity of her legal fees lies squarely with
Plaintiff who chose to embark on a war which was senseless and cruel.

[
95
]

The claim for provision for legal costs is refused.

1-      R. K.
and D. D. are hereby granted a divorce which shall take effect on the 31
st

day from these presents;

2-      That
custody of the two minor children S. D. and A. D. is granted to the Defendant D.
D.;

3-      That R.
K. is granted the following rights of access to A. and S.:

a-On alternating weeks, from Thursday when she will pick the children up from
school to Monday morning when she will drive them to school;

b-During the week preceding a weekend without visiting rights, on Thursday

when she will pick the children up from school to Friday morning when she will
drive them to school;

c-With regard to the Christmas holidays, each parent shall have one
week during this period, including either Christmas or New Years Day on an
alternating basis each year;

d-As to the Easter holidays or spring break, it shall be alternating
from year to year; for the year 2006, R. K. shall have the option which must be
exercised by a thirty day notice to D. D. preceeding the first of the two
holidays.

e-With regard to the summer vacation period, the children should
spend two non consecutive “vacation” weeks with each parent, the rest of the
summer continuing on the same alternating weekly schedule as they have during
the year;

f-On Father’s Day, the children shall spend the day with their
father from 9:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. and reciprocally, on Mother’s Day, they
shall spend the day with their mother for the same period of time, regardless
of the regular residential schedule;

g-With regard to statutory holidays, these should be shared equally
on an alternating basis such that if the children are with their mother on
Labour Day, then they shall be with their father on the next statutory holiday;

h-With respect
to the Jewish holidays, the children should spend one day and night of Rosh
Hashanah with each parent and the first two days of Passover should be shared
equally as well. With regard to Yom Kippur, the children should spend the first
night of Yom Kippur with one parent and stay with that parent until 3:00 p.m.
and they should spend from 3:00 p.m. until the next morning with the other
parent, all on an annual alternating basis;

4-      That D.
D. and R. K. cooperate to the greatest extent possible on matters concerning
education, extracurricular activities, medical and psychological treatment for
both S. and A.; however, in the event of dispute on any of the aforementioned
subjects, the opinion of D. D. shall prevail;

5-      That
the family patrimony shall be divided according to law;

6-      That
the common domicile at […A], Town A, and the country house at […B], Town B, be
listed for sale immediately and sold so soon as is practicable thereafter, with
the proceeds of the sales to be partitioned equally amongst Plaintiff and
Defendant.

7-      Plaintiff's
claim in respect of a minority shareholder’s oppression remedy is hereby
dismissed;

8-      Plaintiff's
claim for a Compensatory allowance is hereby dismissed;

9-      That
Defendant pay to the Plaintiff a lump sum in the amount of $100,000.00;

10-   Plaintiff's
claim for provision for costs is dismissed.
